titre: To catalyze is to speed up what was already possible
accroche: Berzelius christens catalysis in 1835 without explaining it. For Ostwald, Nobel 1909, the notion of reaction rate was still missing.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the 1820s, Döbereiner turns platinum sponge into a hydrogen lighter, which sells well. The metal ignites the gas, then stays intact. A substance triggers a reaction without being consumed in it, and Berzelius sets out to find what these cases have in common.

## A name without an explanation

In 1835, in his annual report, Berzelius brings together disparate cases. Malt turns starch into sugar (Kirchhoff, 1814). Platinum or manganese dioxide decomposes hydrogen peroxide (Thénard, 1818). Sulfuric acid forms ether (Mitscherlich, 1834). Finely divided platinum acts on mixtures of flammable gases (Davy, 1817; Döbereiner, 1823).

The common point, Ostwald sums up in his Nobel lecture of December 12, 1909: the substances do not react on their own, but only after the addition of a substance that is not consumed. Mitscherlich spoke of contact action. Berzelius chooses “catalysis,” “catalyst,” “catalytic force,” and specifies that he claims to explain nothing: this force awakens affinities that were dormant at the given temperature, by the mere presence of the substance.

## Why the idea took poorly

Liebig contradicts Berzelius: for him, a substance in the process of decomposing can drag others along with it. Liebig's definition, less perfect but explicit, wins out for a time. Ostwald gives the reason. The notion of reaction rate was not available. Reactions between salts are so fast that their duration still escapes measurement, and slow reactions pass for annoying anomalies. Even the study by Clément and Désormes in 1806, on sulfuric acid formed with nitrogen oxides, accounts for the promotion of the reaction only uncertainly.

## Rate first

The notion comes from Wilhelmy, a German physicist, in connection with the inversion of cane sugar. Biot and Persoz had observed with the polarimeter that a sugar solution that turns polarized light to the right turns it to the left when a dilute acid is added, and that this takes time. Wilhelmy defines the reaction rate: the quantity transformed relative to time, that is, the derivative of the quantity with respect to time. According to Ostwald, the first article to state this concept is also the first quantitative study of a catalyzed process.

He himself takes it up in 1883. To measure chemical affinity, he follows the decomposition of esters, among them methyl acetate, by hydrochloric acid, watching the acidity of the solution rise. From it he will draw his conception of catalysis: accelerations of processes that are possible and already under way. The 1909 Nobel Prize in Chemistry rewards his work on catalysis, as well as his research on the principles of chemical equilibrium and reaction rates.

## The shift

This definition rules out certain expectations. A catalyst does not open a path that was closed: the process must already be able to occur, that is, lead toward a state of lower free energy, and Ostwald notes that Berzelius had understood this, his definition not contradicting the second law of thermodynamics. The catalyst changes the time required, not the destination: according to the online encyclopedia, it does not change the equilibrium constant, because if it shifted it, it would be a perpetual motion machine.

Ostwald criticizes only one point in Berzelius: action “by mere presence.” The catalyst takes part in intermediate reactions, whose sum does not contain it, a hypothesis of Clément and Désormes that no principle has surpassed until then. And Ostwald sides with Berzelius's warning: a hasty explanation would do harm, and half a century of sterility in this field, followed by an abundant harvest, has shown it. As for how a catalyst acts in each reaction, the question arises case by case.

repere.texte: Ostwald conceives of catalysis as the acceleration of possible processes that are under way, and recalls that the first article stating the notion of reaction rate (Wilhelmy, inversion of sugar) is also the first quantitative study of a catalyzed reaction.

carte.punch: A catalyst makes nothing possible: it speeds up what already was.
carte.idee: Berzelius names catalysis in 1835 without explaining it. The notion of reaction rate was missing, and Wilhelmy supplies it by studying the inversion of sugar. For Ostwald (Nobel 1909), a catalyst speeds up possible processes; it does not make them possible.

quiz.question: What does a catalyst do, according to the conception Ostwald defends?
choix: It makes possible a transformation that could not take place without it
It supplies the reaction with the free energy it lacks to go to completion
It speeds up a process that is already possible, which would happen on its own but too slowly
It drives the reaction toward a more stable state than the one it would reach alone
quiz.explication: Ostwald speaks of accelerations of possible processes already under way: the first choice is therefore wrong, a catalyst does not make possible what was not. It supplies no free energy and does not lead to a more stable state, since the equilibrium does not move: the destination stays the same, it is the length of the trip that changes.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why, according to Ostwald, could catalysis not be understood in the time of Berzelius and Liebig?
choix: Because the notion of reaction rate did not yet exist
Because platinum, the only known catalyst, was too rare to be studied
Because Berzelius had refused to publish the details of his experiments
Because Liebig had proved that catalysts act only on gases
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Ostwald writes that a rational understanding of catalysis depended on the creation of the concept of reaction rate. The known cases were not limited to platinum or to gases, and Berzelius had published his cases in his annual reports.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which reaction served as the textbook case for defining reaction rate?
choix: The decomposition of hydrogen peroxide on manganese dioxide
The combustion of hydrogen on a platinum sponge
The transformation of starch into sugar by malt
The inversion of cane sugar under the action of a dilute acid
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Wilhelmy defined the reaction rate in connection with the inversion of cane sugar, which Biot and Persoz had followed with the polarimeter. The other cases, all catalytic, had been brought together by Berzelius but not used to establish the concept.
